body:
## Problem

Every 429 is classified as permanently fatal, regardless of what the provider actually said.

`work-driver-failure-taxonomy.ts:70`:

```ts
if (isRateLimit429Msg(msg)) {
  return { cause: "rate-limited:429", shouldRetry: false, maxRetries: 0 };
}
```

with the operator-facing string *"provider rate-limited (429) — retrying cannot help"* (`:108`, `:137`) and the comment *"Retrying is definitionally useless."*

But the provider hands us the discriminator in the message. `types.ts:105` documents the observed shape verbatim:

```
"Provider request error: Server requested 86399s retry delay (max: 60s). 429 status code (no body)"
```

Both of these are treated identically today:

| Observed message | Reality | Current handling |
|---|---|---|
| `Server requested 60s retry delay` | per-minute token bucket, clears in a minute | cycle dies |
| `Server requested 86399s retry delay` | daily quota, clears tomorrow | cycle dies |

The retry-delay seconds are never parsed. `RATE_LIMIT_429_PATTERN` matches string *ordering*, not magnitude.

## Why this is the highest-value fix available

Forensic census of 22 `/work` cycles on this machine (`.pi/work-state/*.json` + 21 Pi session transcripts):

- **11 of 16 operator-visible failures (69%) are provider infrastructure**, not code quality. Exactly **one** was a genuine verification failure.
- 6 were 429s specifically; 5 were transport severance.
- Issue #279's cycle died on a 60-second-class 429 and left **11 unrelated issues unstarted**.
- Cost of one such death: #279 burned **$7.08** across three transcripts that produced no committed work.

The operator's own words on re-running it: *"try again, the 429 is also per minute stuff"* — a human correctly classified in seconds what the driver cannot express at all.

## What to build

Replace the binary `{shouldRetry, maxRetries}` with a class enum driven by the parsed delay:

| Signal | Class | Action |
|---|---|---|
| requested delay ≤ threshold (default 300s) | `TRANSIENT_BURST` | sleep the requested delay + jitter, resume the SAME step |
| requested delay > threshold | `QUOTA_WINDOW` | halt with a cap naming the wake time — not a generic failure |
| spend-cap / billing wording | `QUOTA_TERMINAL` | halt + notify; retrying genuinely cannot help |
| transport severance / 5xx / timeout | `TRANSPORT` | capped exponential backoff + **full jitter**, own budget |
| subagent completed, work is wrong | `SEMANTIC` | the only class that may consume the issue's attempt budget |

Also:

- **An infra fault must never decrement the semantic attempt counter.** `step-router.ts:192`'s RETRY_ONCE branch never consults `classification.shouldRetry`, so a 429 on `adversarial` burns the semantic retry and the next failure — of any kind — halts.
- **Full jitter on all backoff.** Mandatory before parallel groups land (#289): N cycles hitting the same 429 would otherwise resynchronise into a thundering herd against the same provider.
- Handoff/`explainCap` text keyed to the class, so a `QUOTA_WINDOW` halt says when to come back instead of "retrying cannot help".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Server requested 60s retry delay … 429` classifies `TRANSIENT_BURST`; `86399s` classifies `QUOTA_WINDOW`. Asserted against the verbatim strings captured in the state files.
- [ ] A `TRANSIENT_BURST` sleeps approximately the requested delay and re-runs the same step, without consuming the semantic budget.
- [ ] A 429 with no parseable delay keeps today's conservative behaviour (halt) rather than guessing.
- [ ] Backoff has full jitter; two classifications of the same fault do not produce the same delay.
- [ ] Sleep is injectable so the offline suite never actually waits.
- [ ] `explainCap` renders a class-specific cause; no 429 reaches the "raise your spawn timeout" boilerplate.

## Out of scope

- The aggregate wall-clock ceiling across retry attempts — that is #357.
- Queue-level continuation past a failed cycle (dead-letter semantics) — separate issue, needs #289's queue.
title: fix(work-driver): every 429 is treated as fatal — the provider's requested retry delay is never parsed (69% of observed failures)
